## Abstract
The GEO Series GSE309890 focuses on the impact of the antidepressant sertraline on antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655. The study explores metabolic changes that contribute to this resistance, particularly the role of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) and the transketolase A (tktA) enzyme. The dataset contains expression profiling by high throughput sequencing from 6 samples. Supplementary files including processed expression values are available for download. This dataset is significant because it offers insights into modifiable metabolic traits linked to antibiotic resistance under SSRI exposure.

## I. Introduction
Background: The study investigates how the antidepressant sertraline biases the emergence of antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli by metabolic rewiring of the pentose phosphate pathway. This is relevant for understanding and potentially mitigating risks of antibiotic resistance in SSRI users.

Literature Review: No linked PubMed publications are registered for this GEO dataset.

Knowledge Gap: The metabolic mechanisms by which SSRIs influence antibiotic resistance were unclear before this study.

Objective & Hypothesis: To analyze gene expression changes in E. coli exposed to sertraline and link metabolic pathway shifts to resistance phenotypes.

## II. Materials and Methods
Study Design: GEO Series GSE309890 was queried to obtain metadata and downloadable files. The study comprises expression profiling by high throughput sequencing using platform GPL24659 on Escherichia coli.

Materials: Data retrieved from NCBI GEO through the GEO Series API.

Procedures: The accession GSE309890 was searched specifying file listing to retrieve metadata and supplementary files.

Statistical Analysis: Not applicable for metadata retrieval.

## III. Results

|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Title                      | Antidepressant sertraline biases resistance emergence via stress-driven rewiring of the pentose phosphate pathway: tktA enables metabolic rollback |
| Organism                   | Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655                                            |
| Experiment Type            | Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing                                   |
| Publication Date           | 2026/02/01                                                                          |
| Sample Count               | 6                                                                                    |
| Platform                   | GPL24659                                                                             |
| Supplementary File Types   | CSV                                                                                  |
| Supplementary Files        | GSE309890_FPKMs_allSamples.csv.gz (510 KB, last modified 2025-11-14)                 |
| FTP Download URL           | https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE309nnn/GSE309890/                         |
| Supplementary Files URL    | https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE309nnn/GSE309890/suppl/                   |
| PubMed linked record       | None                                                                                 |

## IV. Discussion
Interpretation: The dataset contains high throughput expression profiles revealing sertraline-induced metabolic changes in E. coli related to antibiotic resistance. The single available supplementary file provides processed expression values for all samples.

Context: The study is not yet published or indexed in PubMed, but the metadata suggests an important mechanistic insight into SSRI-induced antibiotic resistance.

Limitations: The dataset summary does not provide direct experimental results; the user must download the supplementary CSV for processed expression data. No linked literature is available to contextualize further.

Conclusion & Future Directions: GSE309890 is a resource for analyzing metabolic rewiring in E. coli under sertraline treatment. Downloading and analyzing the supplementary file may uncover gene expression patterns linked to resistance. Future questions include identifying specific gene markers of PPP activation and exploring therapeutic adjuvants.

[2] Supplementary files FTP: https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/series/GSE309nnn/GSE309890/suppl/
